title: Span and Memory (including C# 14 conversions)
hook: Span<T> is a stack-only view over contiguous memory — arrays, stackalloc buffers, or unmanaged pointers — without copying. Memory<T> is the heap-storable counterpart you can put in fields when Span cannot be stored on the heap.

blocks.text: Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T> are ref struct types that reference a memory region with length. Slice without allocating a new array. Memory<T> wraps similar semantics but is a regular struct you can store in async fields. C# 14 improves span conversions and overload resolution for common parsing scenarios. Use spans for parsing, formatting, and protocol work without substring allocations.

entries.plainDefinition: Ref struct view over contiguous memory; cannot be stored on the heap.
Heap-friendly buffer abstraction; use Memory<T> in async fields.
Struct that must live on the stack; cannot be boxed or used as class fields.
entries.example: Span<int> cannot be a field on a heap class without Memory<T> wrapper.

blocks.text: High-concurrency APIs parsing headers and tokens allocate less when they slice spans instead of Substring. Module 14 allocation traps — string concat and Substring — have span-based fixes. Interviewers ask Span versus string: Span is a window; string is an immutable heap object.

blocks.title: Span rules
blocks.body: Span cannot be async method locals that cross await unless converted to Memory. Use Memory<T> or copy to array for fields.

snippet.label: Slice without Substring
snippet.explanation: No new string objects for each slice — reduces gen-0 pressure versus Substring chains.

snippet.label: Memory for async fields
snippet.explanation: Memory<byte> can live in a field and be used with ReadAsync. Span cannot be stored across awaits in the same way.

snippet.label: TryParse on span
snippet.explanation: Guid.TryParse overloads accept ReadOnlySpan<char> — auth token parsing without extra strings.

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Storing Span in a class field — compile error. Using span after underlying array is returned to pool. Assuming span works across await without Memory conversion.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: compare gen-0 allocation rate before and after replacing Substring with AsSpan on a hot auth header parser — dotnet-counters System.Runtime gen-0-gc-count should drop. The JavaScript bridge: ArrayBuffer is a fixed byte slab; Uint8Array.subarray and TextEncoder.encodeInto map directly to ReadOnlySpan<byte> and Utf8.TryWrite in C#. When a WASM or Node addon hands you bytes, treat them like Memory<byte> with explicit lifetime — detached ArrayBuffer is the JS analogue of returning an ArrayPool buffer while a Span still references it.

snippet.label: ArrayBuffer / TextEncoder mental model — UTF-8 span bridge
snippet.explanation: Lines 7–8: C# stackalloc + GetBytes mirrors TextEncoder.encodeInto into ArrayBuffer. Line 11: Slice on span matches Uint8Array.subarray — shared backing, no new allocation.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Hold ArrayBuffer reference — detached on transfer

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Storing Span<T> in a class field — compile error for good reason. Using span after ArrayPool.Return — same as using detached ArrayBuffer in JS. Saying Span works across await without converting to Memory. Not knowing TextEncoder.encodeInto maps to writing into a byte span.

interviewTakeaways: Span<T> is a stack-only ref struct view; Memory<T> is the heap-storable async-friendly counterpart.
ArrayBuffer + Uint8Array.subarray + TextEncoder.encodeInto map to stackalloc/Memory<byte> + Span.Slice + UTF8 GetBytes.
In production, dotnet-counters gen-0 drops when Substring chains become AsSpan + TryParse on auth headers.
60s: Span slices without alloc. Memory for async fields. JS ArrayBuffer = byte backing; subarray = Slice; encodeInto = write UTF-8 into span. Detached buffer = use-after-free trap.
Follow-up: why cannot Span be a field on a class but Memory can?
commonPitfalls: Span as instance field on a class gets you rejected — ref struct cannot live on heap.
Use-after-free when backing array returned to pool while span still references it — like detached ArrayBuffer.
Strong answer: 'Span for hot parse. Memory for async. JS bridge: ArrayBuffer backing, subarray = Slice, TextEncoder = UTF-8 into byte span. Profile gen-0 after Substring removal.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: ArrayBuffer is the backing slab; subarray creates a view without copying — identical mental model to Span<byte>.Slice. postMessage transfer detaches the buffer like returning an ArrayPool array while a span still points at it.

encodeInto writes UTF-8 into an existing Uint8Array without allocating a new buffer. C# Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes(ReadOnlySpan<char>, Span<byte>) and Utf8.TryWrite are the same zero-extra-buffer pattern for protocol headers.
